title: How to write Amazon product descriptions with AI
summary: Learn how to write Amazon product descriptions with AI: build a product brief, generate drafts for every variant, and check each one against your images.
body_markdown:
Amazon product descriptions need to do more than describe a product. They need to give shoppers useful information, match the exact product and variant shown in the listing, support the image gallery and bullets, and follow Amazon's current content requirements.


[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) **helps sellers turn product information into a first draft without writing every description from scratch.** Start with verified facts about the exact product, generate the description with AI, then check the output against your images and product data before publishing.


This becomes particularly useful when you manage multiple products. As your catalog scales, getting products live requires creating more descriptions faster—without losing consistency or introducing details that don't belong to a specific SKU.


This guide explains what belongs in an Amazon product description, how to build a product brief and turn it into a first draft with Photoroom's Product Description Generator, and how to keep descriptions accurate across images, variants, and product updates.


## Table of Contents


## What belongs in an Amazon product description?


An Amazon product description should explain what the title, bullets, and images can't. That includes how the product is used, cared for, set up, or stored, plus any context that helps shoppers decide whether it's right for them. It shouldn't repeat the facts shoppers have already seen higher on the page.


Before generating an Amazon product description, it helps to know what each part of the listing already does.


Listing element Its main job What belongs there


Product title Identify the product Product type, defining attributes, and variation


About this item Help shoppers qualify it quickly Dimensions, material, quantity, compatibility, and important limitations


Product description Explain the product in more detail Use cases, setup, care, storage, and context that explains the facts in the bullets


Image gallery Show the product Appearance, scale, texture, construction, components, and use


A+ Content Expand the product story for eligible sellers Visual explanation, comparisons, and additional brand content


Purchase-critical facts may belong in the “About this item” bullets. For example, a bullet for leather ankle boots could establish: Runs half a size small, order half a size up.


The description can then provide the explanation and context that would be too much information in a short bullet, like how the leather softens with wear and whether the fit works for wider feet or thicker socks.


Understanding this split will help you evaluate how to organize information for Amazon’s requirements and to better serve the shopper.


## How to build a product brief for Amazon product descriptions


Collect the facts that define the product. An AI generator can only work with the information you give it. If the inputs are vague, incomplete, or borrowed from a similar product, the draft will repeat those problems, and you'll spend the time you saved correcting it.


Consider the information the shopper needs to understand what your product is, why it’s relevant to them, and what they’ll receive when it arrives. If there are common objections or complaints about the product—for example, a shirt runs small or a lamp doesn’t include a bulb—record those, too.


[Your product images](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/amazon-product-images) are also useful here. They can help you identify characteristics that need to remain consistent between the copy and what shoppers actually see.


### A product brief template for Amazon descriptions


Then place this information within a product brief. The brief covers more than the description field. It's the reference for your title, bullets, images, and[any other marketplace where you sell the product](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/multichannel-product-image-optimization) .


Input What to record Example (Rain jacket)


Product facts Verified material, size, fit, capacity, compatibility, included items, care or setup information, or other specifications Polyester shell with a water-repellent finish, adjustable hood, two zip hand pockets, packs into its own chest pocket. Sizes XS–XXL. Machine wash cold.


Buyer need What the buyer wants the product to help them do Stay dry during light rain on commutes and walks, then pack the jacket into a bag when the weather clears.


Differentiator A meaningful reason this product is different Folds into its own chest pocket, so it takes up little space in a backpack or tote.


Objection What could make someone hesitate Shoppers ask whether to size up so the jacket fits over a sweater.


Proof The specification, construction detail, or other evidence supporting the benefit Garment measurements for each size (chest, length, sleeve) and the water-resistance rating from the supplier spec sheet.


Variant fields Facts that change between variants Size (chest, length, and sleeve measurements for each) and color name, with images for each colorway. Material, hood, pockets, and care stay the same across variants.


Claims to avoid Statements that sound appealing but can't be verified, or that contradict the product facts "Waterproof" (water-resistant only; seams aren't taped), "breathable" (no breathability rating on record), and "all-weather" (not insulated).


Use these approved inputs to generate and review your Amazon product description. This helps you speed up the production description writing process, while keeping individual listings grounded in the products you actually sell.


## How to use Photoroom's Product Description Generator for Amazon listings


[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) is built specifically for e‑commerce. Instead of writing a prompt, you select a channel, enter your product information, and choose a brand voice and length. Because every description starts from the same fields and settings, a team can generate copy for each variant or marketplace from the same brief without the drift that comes from everyone writing their own prompts.


### 1. Give the generator specific product information


Generic inputs tend to produce generic descriptions.


**Instead of supplying only:**


Lightweight rain jacket


**Use the product brief** to give the generator the details that matter:


Lightweight rain jacket, polyester shell with a water-repellent finish (water-resistant, seams not taped), adjustable hood, two zip hand pockets, packs into its own chest pocket. Sizes XS–XXL; shoppers often ask whether to size up to wear it over a sweater. Machine wash cold. For commutes and walks in light rain. Do not describe as waterproof, breathable, or all-weather.


Generate from the product you are selling, not from a generic version of the product category.


### 2. Choose brand voice and length


Then set the brand voice. For the rain jacket, a useful voice instruction might be:


Practical and direct. Describe when and how the jacket is worn. No superlatives or weather guarantees. Say "water-resistant," not "rainproof."


You can also choose a preset voice from the dropdown. A preset keeps descriptions consistent when several people work on the same catalog.


For length, select an option on the drop-down menu:


-


**Choose short** for familiar products where the images show most of what matters


-


**Choose medium** for products with one or two questions to answer


-


**Choose long** for products with detailed specifications, setup, or compatibility information


### 3. Select Amazon as the channel


Select the channel your description will appear on. In this case,[Amazon](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/sell-on-amazon) .


[The Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) creates your copy based on whichever marketplace you’re selling on: Amazon,[Shopify](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/shopify-product-descriptions-how-to-write-and-scale-better-copy) ,[Etsy](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-write-etsy-product-descriptions-as-your-shop-grows) , or eBay. There’s also an option for a general marketplace category. Small businesses selling on more than one platform can use the same product brief to produce a description for each marketplace, so expanding beyond Amazon doesn't mean rewriting your catalog from scratch.


Amazon requirements can vary by category, marketplace, and listing template and can change over time.[Check the current requirements](https://sellercentral.amazon.com/) before publishing.


### 4. Check the draft against the product images


Read the generated description alongside the final image gallery.


The description should cover what the photos can't show, such as dimensions, care, or what's included, without spending sentences on what the images already make obvious. If the draft doesn't cover key details images can’t show, add them to your input and regenerate.


Then look for contradictions, such as a matte finish in the copy next to a glossy product in the photos, a lifestyle prop described as included, or a color or quantity that belongs to a different variant. The copy and images should describe the same product the customer will receive.


When the copy and an image disagree, check the brief to see which is wrong. If it's the copy, fix the input and regenerate. Photoroom's AI tools can help with[background removal](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) ,[resizing](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-resizer) , and[secondary product images](https://www.photoroom.com/ai-product-photography) , so the gallery shows the product the description describes.


### 5. Use the generated description as a first draft


The Product Description Generator removes the blank-page work and gives you a structured draft based on the product. It’s a starting point, not the final output, and should be reviewed for usefulness and accuracy.


For Amazon,[the Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) returns a short overview followed by bullet points. Before you publish, decide where each part of the generated description goes. The bullets belong in "About this item," where shoppers scan for the purchase-critical facts. The overview opens your product description, which you can expand with context the bullets don't cover.


Then read the draft against the brief, line by line. AI-generated copy can sound convincing even when what it says hasn’t been verified. Every specification should match a product fact, and nothing from the claims-to-avoid row should appear. If you can’t trace a statement back to verified product information, remove it.


When something is wrong, decide whether to edit or regenerate. Fix a single awkward sentence by hand. If the same problem appears in every draft, such as a sizing note that's always missing, update the input and regenerate instead. That way the fix carries into every variant and channel you generate from the same brief.


## How to use AI to create Amazon product descriptions for every variant


[Creating accurate product descriptions](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-write-product-descriptions-that-sell-online) for variants is where many e‑commerce businesses struggle as their product catalog scales. On Amazon, sizes and colors are often grouped into a variation family under one parent listing. That makes it harder to identify errors in duplicated copy.


Someone working on the listing adds a new size, copies the existing description, and updates only the measurements in the first line. The capacity, included pieces, or care details further down still describe the original. Reviews are typically shared across variants, so a "not as described" complaint about one variant can affect how shoppers see all of them.


Inconsistency costs trust, too. In Photoroom's 2026 marketplace research,[63% of 2,000 UK consumers](https://www.photoroom.com/industry-trends/state-of-genai-in-marketplaces-2026) said inconsistent product images, styles, or branding across listings can make a seller seem unreliable. When variants in the same family describe the product differently, or show it differently, shoppers notice.


[The Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) eliminates much of the writing work that creates the need to copy and paste descriptions from one variant to another. For each variant, update only the variant-specific fields in the product brief. Then generate a new description with Amazon selected and the same brand voice and length settings.


Review each draft against the brief and that variant's own images, not against the description you generated before it, so an error in one version doesn't carry into the next. If a new colorway doesn't have its own photos yet,[Photoroom's Recolor tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) can[create variant images from an existing product photo](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-product-color-variants-without-reshooting) . Check the result against the physical product, since the color name in the copy and the color in the image need to match what the customer receives.


If a variant differs in construction or materials rather than just size or color, give it its own brief instead of treating it as a variation of the original.


## How to update Amazon product descriptions when product details change


New listings aren't the only source of inaccurate copy. Products change after launch. A supplier switches a fabric, revises a size chart, or drops an included accessory, and the descriptions written for the original version stay live.


Update the affected facts in the brief first. Then regenerate each affected description in[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) with the same channel, brand voice, and length settings you used originally, and review each one against the updated brief.


Check the images too. A change in fabric, color, or other visual identifiers could require[updated supplier imagery](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-edit-supplier-photos-e-commerce) to make the entire product listing accurate.


If you sell the product on other marketplaces, like[Shopify](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/shopify-product-descriptions-how-to-write-and-scale-better-copy) or Etsy, regenerate those versions from the same updated brief so every channel describes the product you're currently shipping.


## Review your AI-generated Amazon description before publishing


Every generated description should receive a final product-level review. Maintaining one Amazon description checklist across your entire catalog can keep product descriptions consistent, especially when multiple people are working at different times across multiple listings.


### Check the inputs


-


The brief matches the exact SKU and variant


-


Variant-specific fields were updated before generating


-


The same brand voice and length settings were used across the variation family


### Check the output


-


Every specification matches the brief


-


Nothing from the claims-to-avoid row appears


-


Photographed props are not described as included


-


Prohibited promotional or testimonial language has been removed


-


Bullets go in "About this item," and the overview opens the description


If a check fails because of a one-off phrase, edit it. If it fails because of the inputs, such as a wrong measurement or a missing sizing note, fix the brief and regenerate. Otherwise the same error will appear in the next variant or channel you generate.


If an image changes before publication, check whether the copy in the product description still matches it. If the copy changes, check that the images still accurately represent what the copy says. An AI generated product description becomes publishable only after the product, images, and copy agree.
